metaData.title: AI Agent & Skill Evaluation: A Framework and Practical Implementation
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: This article systematically introduces the Tencent TEG team's practical framework for evaluating AI Agents, proposing a comprehensive evaluation system composed of three types of scorers: deterministic scorers, rubric scorers, and human scorers, covering five dimensions—functional correctness, process quality, efficiency and cost, robustness and safety, and experience alignment—validated through the TPerf performance analysis Agent project.
metaData.summary: Starting from three major pain points of AI Agents in production environments—non-determinism, black-box nature, and cascading error amplification—the article argues for the necessity of establishing an automated evaluation system. Its core contribution is a complete evaluation framework: first, it defines a combination strategy of 'deterministic scorer + rubric scorer + human scorer,' clarifying their respective application scenarios and priorities; second, it breaks down evaluation dimensions into five categories—functional correctness, process quality, efficiency and cost, robustness and safety, and experience alignment—providing sub-items, evaluation methods, and typical indicators for each dimension. On the implementation level, the article details four scenarios for test case design (triggering, core logic, output quality, and error tolerance), a negative scoring system, baseline establishment and update mechanisms, and key engineering issues (trace output, environment isolation, stability assessment, report generation). Finally, using the TPerf performance AI analysis Agent as a practical case study, it demonstrates how to apply the general methodology to create specific scoring criteria, case organization, and baseline management processes. The article is clearly structured with detailed examples, serving as a directly reusable practical guide for Agent evaluation.

mainPoints.point: Agent evaluation must adopt a combination of 'deterministic scorer + rubric scorer + human scorer.'
mainPoints.explanation: A single evaluation method cannot address both the hard indicators (e.g., file existence, correct calls) and soft indicators (e.g., reasoning quality, suggestion quality) of Agent outputs. The three types of scorers have different focuses, with a priority order of deterministic > rubric > human.

mainPoints.point: Evaluation dimensions should cover five categories: functional correctness, process quality, efficiency and cost, robustness and safety, and experience alignment.
mainPoints.explanation: These five dimensions progress from 'did it do it right?' to 'is it user-friendly?' P0 prioritizes functional correctness and robustness/safety, P1 covers process quality and efficiency/cost, and P2 supplements experience and alignment as needed.

mainPoints.point: Test case design must cover four scenarios: triggering, core logic, output quality, and error tolerance, with core logic cases being the most numerous.
mainPoints.explanation: Each scenario includes both positive and negative test cases. Core logic cases need to cover each business branch flow chart one by one, and their quantity is typically 2-3 times the sum of the other three scenario types.

mainPoints.point: Baseline management is the core of the evaluation system, establishing expected processes and outcomes through a 'run first, then confirm' approach.
mainPoints.explanation: A baseline is a snapshot of expected results for a single test case, confirmed manually after its first execution. Every subsequent execution is compared against this baseline, serving both the deterministic and rubric scorers.

mainPoints.point: The evaluation system should distinguish between capability evaluation and regression evaluation; once capability cases achieve stable pass rates, they 'graduate' to the regression suite.
mainPoints.explanation: Capability evaluation guides optimization directions, while regression evaluation prevents drift. The regression test set only grows, and CI runs it every time.

keyQuotes: Eval = Agent Input → Execution → Capture Execution Process (Trace + Output) → A Set of Check Rules → Comparable Scores
Use code for judgment whenever possible, use models when necessary, and use humans for calibration.
Every change should quickly produce a comparable score, replacing intuition with data and spot checks with full coverage.

relatedArticles.title: Understanding Hermes in One Article: How the New Top-Tier Agent Self-Evolves from Experience
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article provides an in-depth analysis of the core innovation of the Hermes Agent—the Skills closed-loop system—detailing its complete implementation mechanism, from experience extraction and knowledge storage to intelligent retrieval and self-improvement, along with its engineering trade-offs and security considerations.

relatedArticles.title: Harness Engineering: How I Spent a Week Boosting AI Coding Rate to 90% in an Enterprise App
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article systematically introduces Harness Engineering, a new AI coding paradigm that elevates the AI code rate of an enterprise Java application from 25% to over 90% by building a four-element system of rules, skills, knowledge, and change management.

relatedArticles.title: Understanding Harness Engineering: Finding the Shell That Keeps AI from Going Rogue—Insights from 14 Engineering Articles | Hao's Trend Talk
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article provides an in-depth analysis of "Harness Engineering," a core technology in the AI Agent field. It reveals how to compensate for model shortcomings through a three-layer management architecture and proposes the logic of "Compensation Surface Migration" that evolves with model capabilities.

relatedArticles.title: Investing 10,000 RMB in AI: A Year of Tools, Practices, and Reflections
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: A systematic summary of a veteran developer's practical experience in the AI wave, covering everything from MAC toolchain optimization and Harness Engineering architectural constraints to building an Agent-driven automated learning loop.

relatedArticles.title: OpenClaw and Hermes: A Comprehensive Review of AI Agent Architecture from Source Code
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article systematically summarizes the design trade-offs and engineering practices of Agent architecture in core modules such as message routing, memory management, context engineering, and security sandboxing, through an in-depth analysis of the source code of two open-source AI Agent frameworks: OpenClaw and Hermes.

relatedArticles.title: Beyond Cognitive Reconstruction: Stepping into the Engineering Revolution of Agentic Engineering
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article provides a deep dive into the practical journey of Tencent engineers transitioning from Vibe Coding to Agentic Engineering, proposing an AI-assisted engineering system centered on context management and tool-oriented design.

relatedArticles.title: When the Entire Team Goes Zero-Manual Coding: A 10,000-Word AI-Native Development Handbook
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article details the Tencent team's practical experience in transitioning from AI-assisted programming to an AI-native development model, achieving a 'zero-manual coding' development loop through the OpenSpec specification and CodeBuddy toolchain.

relatedArticles.title: Harness Is Not the Goal, Knowledge Is the Moat — Knowledge Accumulation Practices of an AI Engineering Delivery Team
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Based on the engineering delivery practices of an AI Team, this article proposes that knowledge accumulation is more important than workflow orchestration, and systematically introduces a complete methodology encompassing a five-layer knowledge storage architecture, a three-level maturity system, and how workflows serve knowledge accumulation.

relatedArticles.title: From Requirements to Deployment: A Comprehensive Leap in R&D Efficiency with Full AI Automation
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article systematically explains how Tencent's audit team built a fully automated AI delivery platform to achieve end-to-end automation from requirements, design, development, testing to deployment, and shares its evolution path from L2 (human-machine collaboration) to L3 (full automation), along with core challenges, specific practices, and quantified benefits.

relatedArticles.title: AI R&D Automation: Wiki Knowledge Base + Skill Pack
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article details how to build a continuously growing team knowledge base and a supporting expert skill pack based on the LLM-Wiki model and the Obsidian platform to achieve AI-driven R&D automation.
